summary:
Private, adult, consensual conduct between men and between women has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the colonial Penal Code offence at Article 175, which had carried a maximum of fourteen years' imprisonment. Enforcement had already stopped: in July 2006 Fiji's High Commissioner in New Zealand confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested. The enforcement era produced prosecutions — in 2005 an Australian tourist, Thomas McCosker, and a Fijian man, Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year sentences under Article 175, and the trial judge described the acts as 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Those convictions were overturned in August 2005 by Fiji's highest court as violations of the constitution then in force.

The Constitution promulgated in September 2013, Article 26(3)(a), prohibits unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, sexual orientation, and gender identity and expression. The 1997 Constitution had already barred discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, which made Fiji one of the first two countries in the world to do so, alongside South Africa. The Asia Pacific Alliance's 2023 case study describes the 2013 protection on gender identity and expression as unique worldwide.

Statutory layers sit beneath that guarantee. The Employment Relations Promulgation 2007 has prohibited discrimination in employment on grounds of sexual orientation since 2007, and in 2013 the government included sexual orientation and gender identity within anti-hate speech law and within law governing discrimination in certain businesses.

The Mental Health Decree 2010 provides that a person is not mentally ill for refusing or failing to express a particular sexual orientation, and it bars registered mental health professionals from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation. Outright International's overview records the same prohibition on health professionals attempting to change sexual orientation.

Legal gender recognition does not exist. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker, and they do not recognise traditional third-gender identities. The traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa — people assigned male at birth who dress, act and behave as female — has been accepted by Fijian society, but that cultural standing carries no legal route to recognition of gender. The Asia Pacific Alliance records the result as a headline constitutional protection with no implementation for trans people, producing documented marginalisation and discrimination. Intersex bodily autonomy is likewise unprotected.

Fiji provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, and no statutory union other than marriage is available to a couple read as same-sex under birth-sex status. Prime ministerial opposition to any change was restated on 26 March 2013, in January 2016, and in 2019.

Documented violence includes the brutal murder of a young transgender woman in Suva in May 2018, in a setting where mistrust of police, rooted in the risk of harassment, is reported to discourage LGBTQ people and couples from reporting anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination. The dossier's other recorded incidents are older and are historical: the murder of Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener in Suva on 1 July 2001 in an apparent homophobic attack with possible political motive, and a gay student found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. Activists additionally describe physical violence and domestic abuse operating as a form of familial conversion therapy for LGBTQ people. The sources characterise hate-crime reports as rare while listing these cases; no dataset of police-reported incidents is available.

Social climate is shaped by majority Methodist and Catholic denominations, which traditionally view transgender identities negatively, and by a Muslim minority of about 6% that tends to regard cross-dressing as sinful behaviour to be corrected. Social mores on sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative, with little public support for LGBTQ rights, and reports of societal discrimination and bullying are recorded without a figure or period. Public displays of affection are not illegal but are generally considered offensive.

In April 2017 the Ministry of Health confirmed that gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood, following the refusal of a gay man on grounds of his sexual orientation.

Political participation has advanced at one point. In 2022 the National Federation Party endorsed Divina Loloma, a transgender woman, as the first openly LGBTQ candidate ever endorsed by a political party; the leader of the All People's Party, Tuiloma Tawaivuna, denounced the nomination, calling transgender people an 'abomination' and 'Biblically wrong'.

Organising has been permitted as well as obstructed. The government has in the past cancelled gay pride marches, but activists held activities on 17 May 2013 for the international day against homophobia, biphobia and transphobia, an event in Suva in 2017 attended by activists and religious figures, and Fiji's first pride parade on 17 May 2018 in Lautoka, held with a local police escort and addressed by former President Epeli Nailatikau.
tangentialFactors:
Fiji's status as one of the first two countries worldwide to constitutionally bar sexual-orientation discrimination, alongside South Africa in 1997, is a comparative point rather than a measure of present protection: the Asia Pacific Alliance's 2023 study pairs that distinction with the finding that no implementing framework exists for trans people, so constitutional rank and lived legal effect diverge here.

Source eras differ sharply and should not be read together as a single snapshot. The GlobalGayz country page is undated and pre-2013; its claim that sexual orientation and gender identity discrimination was not banned predates the current Constitution. Outright International's overview, updated 12 March 2026, carries an 'at a glance' flag listing same-sex relations as illegal, which conflicts with the 2010 decriminalisation the same page documents.

The political-religious climate behind earlier enforcement is on record: on 14 April 2005 Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in what he described as a conservative Christian nation, days after the two-year sentences were imposed. That statement dates from the enforcement era and predates the 2006 no-arrest policy and the 2010 repeal.

Public organising has moved in both directions within the same period: pride marches have been cancelled by the government, and the 17 May 2018 parade in Lautoka proceeded with a police escort and an address by a former president. Both facts sit in the record without further cancellation or further permit data.
localsOnly:
Residents have an enforceable constitutional complaint under Article 26(3)(a) of the 2013 Constitution for unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, sexual orientation, and gender identity and expression, plus statutory employment protection under the Employment Relations Promulgation 2007 for sexual-orientation discrimination, and the 2013 extension of anti-hate speech and business-discrimination law to sexual orientation and gender identity.

Registered mental health professionals are barred by the Mental Health Decree 2010 from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation, and the decree states that a person is not mentally ill for declining to express a particular sexual orientation. Conversion practices by unregistered actors are not covered by that provision, and activists report familial physical violence and domestic abuse serving the same function.

Resident couples receive no marital or civil-union recognition under the Marriage Act 2002, which limits marriage to one man and one woman. Trans residents have no mechanism to amend a gender marker on any document, and the traditional third-gender identity of vaka sa lewa lewa has no statutory standing.

Gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood under a Ministry of Health position confirmed in April 2017. Mistrust of police because of possible harassment is documented as suppressing reporting of anti-gay violence and discriminatory acts among residents, so recorded incident counts understate what activists describe.

Trans people have stood for office with party endorsement: in 2022 the National Federation Party endorsed Divina Loloma, the first openly LGBTQ candidate endorsed by a political party, drawing public condemnation from the leader of the All People's Party. Intersex bodily autonomy has no statutory protection.
outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's overview page (updated 12 March 2026) carries an 'at a glance' block stating that same-sex relations are illegal, listing legal gender recognition as 'No', and stating that organisations cannot register. The illegality flag contradicts the decriminalisation the same page records for 2010 and is treated here as an unresolved source inconsistency rather than as a current rule. The organisation-registration claim appears in that one source only and is not corroborated or explained elsewhere in the inventory; its meaning (which organisations, under which statute) remains not sourced.

No figures are available for police-reported incidents of anti-LGBTQ violence, for court convictions after 2010, or for the use of the constitutional discrimination guarantee. The characterisation of hate crimes as 'rare' is the source's own wording and carries no count or period, so the true frequency is unresolved.

The inventory contains no information on entry or visa screening, on airport document checks or gender-marker flagging, on detention or immigration handling of trans travellers, or on availability of gender-affirming care, hormone supply, or trans-specific healthcare for visitors. Absence of those items in the sources is not evidence that no issue exists.

Outright's 2026 overview states that health professionals are barred from trying to change sexual orientation, and the Mental Health Decree 2010 wording bars registered mental health professionals; whether unregistered practitioners fall outside the prohibition is not sourced. The scope of the 2013 anti-hate speech provision, including penalties and any prosecution to date, is likewise not stated in the inventory.
